evidence_quotes.quote: In this study, we analyze the relationship between local income inequality and the progressivity of water prices for US utilities that serve populations of 40,000 or more.

Investor-owned utilities must set prices according to the cost of service principle, which limits prices to the actual cost of providing service, plus a fixed return on the utility's capital investment.

Our sample consists of the 1189 utilities that serve at least 40,000 residents according to SDWIS. 134 of these utilities are investor-owned, with prices set by state PUCs; the remaining 1055 utilities are owned and operated by local governments that set their own prices.

We evaluate the relationship between income inequality and water price progressivity using ordinary least squares regression models with robust standard errors, an estimation strategy commonly used in the analysis of residential water prices across utilities

In the absence of such microdata, the dependent variable in the present analysis is the progressivity of water prices, which we measure as the ratio of the average unit price of water at basic consumption levels to the average unit price of water at high volumes.

criterion_notes.c1: Does not empirically examine household or community water or sanitation service access. Instead, the study analyzes public enterprise rate-making as redistributive politics (adapting the Cukierman-Meltzer taxation model), testing whether local income inequality and public versus investor-owned utility status predict the progressivity of residential drinking water rate structures across large US utilities. Although household water affordability is discussed as a policy motivation in the background and conclusion, service access, connection, availability, continuity, consumption, disconnection, and household bill affordability are not empirically examined.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: Yes — alongside its primary socioeconomic predictor (local income inequality), the study explicitly examines an institutional/regulatory governance factor: utility ownership and rate-setting structure (local government-owned utilities whose rates are set legislatively by elected councils/boards versus private investor-owned utilities whose rates are set by state Public Utilities Commissions [PUCs] under quasi-judicial cost-of-service rules). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Utility ownership and PUC cost-of-service regulatory structure fall within the protocol's rule-type categories ('utility ownership or regulatory structure' and 'tariff or cost-recovery rules'), rather than generic project delivery, behavioural promotion, or unanalysed macro-governance background; however, in this paper they are modeled only as determinants/moderators of tariff structure progressivity (Unit Price Ratio) rather than directly governing a measured household service-access outcome, and the primary theoretical exposure is socioeconomic income inequality. Under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4 (wrong outcome).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary quantitative empirical analysis of an original 2019 rate dataset covering 1,189 US community water systems serving at least 40,000 residents (analytic sample N = 1,183 in the contiguous 48 states), matched with US Census ACS and NOAA drought data and estimated via ordinary least squares regressions with robust standard errors.
criterion_notes.c4: No eligible access or affordability outcome is reported. The sole modeled dependent variable is residential tariff structure progressivity, measured by the Unit Price Ratio (UPR): the average unit price per gallon at high monthly volumes (30,000 gallons in main models; 12,000 to 60,000 gallons in sensitivity analyses) divided by the average unit price per gallon at basic household consumption (6,000 gallons monthly). Because UPR is a dimensionless ratio of two points on the same tariff schedule, it is invariant to overall price levels, includes no household income or expenditure-burden measure, and measures tariff policy design (inclining vs. declining block structure) rather than access, connection, service availability, reliability, water quantity consumed, household affordability, or exclusion/disconnection.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis and sample (1,189 US community water utilities serving >=40,000 residents; N = 1,183 in regressions), exposures (service-area mean-to-median income ratio and private investor-owned PUC-regulated vs. local government utility ownership), outcome (2019 single-family residential Unit Price Ratio), and study design (cross-sectional observational OLS regression study) are all clearly specified.

study_design: Cross-sectional quantitative observational study (ordinary least squares regression with robust standard errors)
population_and_sample: US community drinking water utilities serving populations of 40,000 or more (unit of analysis: utility; N = 1,189 sampled from EPA SDWIS serving 183,314,934 residents, comprising 1,055 local government utilities and 134 investor-owned utilities; analytic regression sample N = 1,183 in the contiguous 48 states)
exposure: Service-area income inequality (mean-to-median household income ratio, primary theoretical predictor) and utility ownership/regulatory structure (binary indicator for private investor-owned utilities regulated by state Public Utilities Commissions under cost-of-service rules vs. local government-owned utilities setting their own rates, plus ownership-by-inequality interaction)
outcome: Residential water price progressivity, measured as the Unit Price Ratio (UPR): average unit price per gallon at high monthly consumption volumes (30,000 gallons in main models; 12,000 to 60,000 gallons across auxiliary models) divided by average unit price per gallon at basic household consumption (6,000 gallons monthly)
rationale: Excluded under E04 (Wrong outcome). This political economy paper tests Cukierman and Meltzer's (1991) redistributive taxation model on 2019 single-family residential rate schedules across 1,183 large US community water utilities, examining whether local income inequality and public enterprise versus PUC-regulated investor-owned utility ownership predict tariff progressivity. Although utility ownership and PUC cost-of-service regulation are institutional/regulatory mechanisms, the sole modeled dependent variable is a policy/tariff-design metric — the Unit Price Ratio (UPR), dividing unit price at 30,000 gallons/month by unit price at 6,000 gallons/month. Because UPR cancels out overall price levels and omits household income, expenditure burden, basic bill affordability, consumption quantity, connection, continuity, and disconnection, the study examines determinants of tariff-structure progressivity rather than a water service access or affordability outcome (c1 = no, c4 = no). Statistical significance of individual coefficients played no role in this decision.
